facts.fact: Rosenfeld and Morville's 1998 book brought information architecture into mainstream web practice.
facts.quote: Rosenfeld and Morville’s 1998 book brought information architecture into mainstream web practice, and by 2002

facts.fact: By 2002 the information architecture discipline was commonly framed around navigation, labeling, content organization, and search, according to a systematic review of IA research.
facts.quote: by 2002 the discipline was commonly framed around navigation, labeling, content organization, and search

facts.fact: The website navigation architecture guide lists four connected parts: classification logic, hierarchical structure, labeling, and orientation cues.
facts.quote: ### The Four Connected Parts

facts.fact: The vendor's pattern table recommends a single-level top menu for five to seven clear top items.
facts.quote: | Single-level top menu | Five to seven clear top items |

facts.fact: The vendor advises starting with a single-level menu when a site has under 15 pages and one level.
facts.quote: If you have under 15 pages and one level, start single-level.

facts.fact: The vendor advises using breadcrumb trails on any site deeper than two levels.
facts.quote: | Breadcrumb trail | Orientation on deep pages | Not a primary navigation on its own | Any site deeper than two levels |

facts.fact: The vendor's Twelve Phrase Test has you list the top twelve search phrases a customer would type and confirm each has a page reachable in two clicks.
facts.quote: Confirm each phrase has a page reachable in two clicks.

facts.fact: Google's 2025 guidance says pages reached from classic or AI search must be easy to move through and clearly distinguish the main content, according to the vendor's summary.
facts.quote: Google’s 2025 guidance says pages reached from classic or AI search must be easy to move through and clearly distinguish the main content

facts.fact: WCAG 2.1 requires repeated navigational mechanisms to remain in the same relative order unless the user initiates a change.
facts.quote: WCAG 2.1 requires repeated navigational mechanisms to remain in the same relative order unless the user initiates a change

facts.fact: The vendor advises counting pages, counting levels, and naming the top three actions a visitor must take before choosing a navigation pattern.
facts.quote: Count your pages, count your levels, and name the **top three actions** a visitor must take.

facts.fact: The 2025 Web Almanac accessibility chapter reports that only 31% of mobile sites meet minimum color-contrast requirements.
facts.quote: only 31% of mobile sites meet minimum color-contrast requirements

facts.fact: The 2025 Web Almanac accessibility chapter reports that only about 24% of desktop and mobile pages contain detectable skip links.
facts.quote: only about 24% of desktop and mobile pages contain detectable skip links

facts.fact: The 2025 Web Almanac accessibility chapter reports that median Lighthouse Accessibility scores reached above 85.
facts.quote: median Lighthouse Accessibility scores reached above 85

facts.fact: The article's working flag is that any navigation label where task success falls below roughly 70% should be rewritten and retested.
facts.quote: Rewrite any label where success falls below roughly 70%, retest with new participants

facts.fact: The article recommends listing five to eight high-value tasks as the first step of navigation testing.
facts.quote: List five to eight high-value tasks

facts.fact: The article recommends about 15 people for an open card sort of services.
facts.quote: Ask about 15 people to group and name your services

facts.fact: The article's comparison table lists about 15 participants for a closed card sort.
facts.quote: | Closed card sort | Whether users place items in your categories | About 15 | When testing a proposed structure |

facts.fact: The article's comparison table lists 30 or more participants for a tree test.
facts.quote: | Tree test | Can users find each task in the hierarchy without visuals | 30 or more | Before visual design is final |

facts.fact: The article's comparison table lists 20 to 30 participants for a first-click test.
facts.quote: | First-click test | Where users click first on a page | 20 to 30 | Checking labels on landing and service pages |

facts.fact: The article's comparison table lists 5 to 10 participants per audience type for a task completion check on the live site.
facts.quote: | Task completion check | Whether visitors finish high-value tasks on the live site | 5 to 10 per audience type | After launch and after each change |

facts.fact: A controlled experiment involving 30 participants and five information-seeking tasks found significant completion-time differences for some tasks between architectures, while SUS scores did not differ significantly.
facts.quote: A controlled experiment involving 30 participants and five information-seeking tasks

facts.fact: Baymard's benchmark found 76% of top-grossing U.S. and European e-commerce sites performed at a mediocre level or worse for homepage and category navigation.
facts.quote: Baymard’s benchmark found 76% of top-grossing U.S. and European e-commerce sites performed at a “mediocre” level or worse

facts.fact: Baymard's newer summary reports mediocre-to-poor navigation performance for 61% of desktop sites.
facts.quote: mediocre-to-poor performance for **61% of desktop sites and 65% of mobile sites**

facts.fact: The article's navigation mistakes table flags a top menu with more than seven items as a sign that pages should be grouped under hub pages.
